compounded-vs-ruo-peptides.html:
Peptidemap is a research-use-only (RUO) comparison publisher. It is not a clinic, pharmacy, supplier or drug company. This page explains a regulatory document. It is not medical, legal or purchasing advice, and it does not say that any compounded or RUO product is safe, effective or legal to use.

On 28 Oct 2026 the HHS Office of the Secretary announced a draft "Enforcement Discretion Policy Regarding 503A Compounding Using Certain Peptide Bulk Drug Substances" [1][2] [primary]. It names six peptides: BPC-157, epitalon, KPV, MOTS-c, semax and TB-500 [1] [primary]. The Federal Register notice (FR Doc. 2026-22192, docket HHS-OASH-2026-0496, RIN 0910-ZD94) was filed on 28 Oct and published on 30 Oct 2026 at 91 FR 68526 [2] [primary]. This guide covers who can compound, what the draft does and does not do, and how compounded drugs differ from RUO-labelled peptides.

Who can compound: 503A vs 503B

Compounding is described in the notice as "a practice in which a licensed pharmacist, a licensed physician or, in the case of an outsourcing facility, a person under the supervision of a licensed pharmacist, combines, mixes or alters ingredients of a drug to create a medication tailored to the needs of an individual patient" [2] [primary].

Federal law has two compounding tracks:

  • Section 503A covers drugs compounded "by a licensed pharmacist in a State-licensed pharmacy or Federal facility, or by a licensed physician" [1] [primary]. If certain conditions are met, those drugs are exempt from FDA pre-market approval, the "adequate directions for use" labelling rule, and federal CGMP requirements [1] [primary]. One condition is that each drug must be compounded "based on the receipt of a valid patient specific prescription" [1] [primary]. Another condition limits which bulk ingredients can be used. The ingredient must have a USP or NF monograph, or be a component of an FDA-approved drug, or appear on the 503A Bulks List, which is set through rulemaking [1] [primary].
  • Section 503B covers outsourcing facilities. These are the larger facilities that NPR describes as "producing higher volumes of medicines" [5] [press].

The draft is written for 503A. It names "a State-licensed pharmacy, Federal facility, or licensed physician" as the entities it covers [1] [primary]. Outsourcing facilities are not among the entities it names. NPR reports that the policy "doesn't apply to the larger ones, called 503Bs" [5] [press]. NCPA describes the policy as covering 503A compounding pharmacies [6] [press].

What enforcement discretion does and does NOT mean

The core sentence of the draft says that, in the listed circumstances, "HHS does not intend to take enforcement action against a State-licensed pharmacy, Federal facility, or licensed physician compounding a drug product using a bulk drug substance in Appendix A" [1] [primary].

The documents say this is not:

  • Approval. "Compounded drugs are not FDA-approved, which means FDA does not review their safety, effectiveness, or quality before they are marketed" [1][2] [primary]. HHS cites "the lack of availability of approved products" [2] [primary].
  • A Bulks List listing. The draft applies to substances that are not "on the 503A bulks list codified at 21 CFR 216.23(a)" [1] [primary]. It states that "FDA's future rulemakings may propose adding some or all of these peptides" [2] [primary]. NCPA reports that pharmacies "are still awaiting final rulemaking" [6] [press].
  • Category 1. Appendix B says each of the six was in FDA's interim Category 2 from 2023 "until April 22, 2026" [1] [primary]. None is in Category 1. The HHS draft is a separate policy.
  • Binding or permanent. The notice says the draft "does not establish any rights for any person and is not binding on HHS or the public" [2] [primary]. It gives no end date. It applies "until a peptide bulk drug substance is addressed in a final rule as being included or not included on the 503A bulks list" [1] [primary]. NCPA notes that "no timeframe was given" [6] [press].
  • Irrevocable. "HHS may revisit application of this interim policy (in whole or in part) if, among other things, a safety signal or product quality issue arises" [1][2] [primary].
  • A safety or efficacy finding. The documents contain no determination that any of the six is safe or effective. Appendix B records that for each peptide "CDER recommended against listing" and that the PCAC, which met 23–24 Jul 2026 [4], voted in favour [1] [primary]. The draft was reviewed by OIRA from 14 Oct to 27 Oct 2026 under the title "Interim Access Policy for Compounding Using Certain Peptides" [3] [primary]. NPR reports that FDA's own scientists recommended against unwinding the restrictions [5] [press].

The comment window is "2 weeks after date of publication in the Federal Register," through regulations.gov on docket HHS-OASH-2026-0496 [2] [primary]. Regulations.gov lists the comment period as closing on 13 Nov 2026 at 11:59 pm Eastern Time [10] [primary].

Scope: forms, listed routes and single ingredient

The coverage is narrow. Appendix B defines each covered identity by amino acid sequence, formula and molecular weight [1] [primary]. The forms are BPC-157 acetate, TB-500 acetate, epitalon acetate, KPV acetate, MOTS-c acetate and semax free base. Other salt forms are not listed.

The draft also lists routes. The list below describes the policy's scope only. It is not usage information.

  • BPC-157 acetate: subcutaneous, intramuscular, oral and topical dosage forms
  • TB-500 acetate: subcutaneous or intramuscular injectable dosage forms only
  • MOTS-c acetate: subcutaneous or intramuscular injectable dosage forms
  • Epitalon acetate: subcutaneous or intramuscular injectable dosage forms "dispensed in intermittent courses"
  • Semax free base: intranasal use
  • KPV acetate: topical and oral dosage forms [1] [primary]

The product must contain "only a single Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient (API) listed in Appendix A" [1] [primary]. Blends fall outside the draft. That includes combinations of two listed peptides, such as BPC-157 with TB-500. The only drug delivery device that may be co-packaged with or contain the compounded drug is "an FDA 510(k)-cleared syringe" [1] [primary]. For any oral form, the compounder is expected to keep documentation showing "an adequate level of oral bioavailability in humans" [1] [primary].

Identity, purity and adverse-event conditions, as stated

The draft does not use the word "certify." These are the conditions in its own words [1] [primary]:

  • Identity. The substance "has the identity and limitations in route of administration described in Appendix B. The identity includes but is not limited to amino acid sequence, chemical structure, molecular weight, and molecular formula."
  • Characterization. The substance "is from a facility registered under section 510 … and characterized and identified in a valid certificate of analysis (COA) that includes test results consistent with existing guidance-based criteria described by FDA." HHS says this "helps provide assurance that what a compounder receives from a supplier is what it claims to be and has been tested for identity, purity, potency, and the absence of harmful contaminants such as endotoxins, heavy metals, microbial contamination, and impurities."
  • Original manufacturer. The original manufacturer, "not a subsequent packer, repacker, labeler, or distributor," must be registered under section 510 and comply with CGMP. Its facility location must be listed on the COA. An FDA-registered repacker or reseller must itself document "vendor validation" of the manufacturer and its COA. The COA requirements include the grade "Intended for human drug compounding."
  • Reporting. Compounders must "report products compounded, serious adverse events, and product quality issues to FDA and to the States where the products are compounded and sent (if different)." Serious adverse events must be reported "regardless of whether or not considered drug related," and product-quality issues as well, to FDA's MedWatch program. Product reports must include the active ingredient and its strength, the original manufacturer with its facility identifier, and the dosage form and route. The reporting procedure "should be detailed on the product labeling provided to the patient."
  • Label. The label must state: "This is a compounded drug product. Not for resale."
  • Other law. The product must comply with "all other applicable requirements of the FD&C Act," including the insanitary-conditions ban and "section 503A's … patient specific prescription requirement."

How this differs from RUO-labelled products

RUO ("research use only") products are sold with a label saying they are not for human use. The draft's conditions describe a different channel:

  • Labelling. Covered compounded products carry the statement "This is a compounded drug product. Not for resale" [1] [primary]. RUO products carry research-only labelling.
  • Intended use. The draft covers drug products compounded for an individual patient under section 503A [1] [primary]. RUO labelling states that a product is not intended for human use.
  • Prescription. The draft requires a valid patient-specific prescription [1] [primary]. No prescription is involved in RUO sales.
  • Identity and purity oversight. The draft ties coverage to a 510-registered, CGMP-compliant original manufacturer, a COA meeting FDA-referenced testing criteria, and MedWatch reporting [1] [primary]. RUO products are outside these terms, and none of the draft's identity, purity or reporting conditions apply to them.

HHS's stated rationale refers to RUO directly. The Secretary "has determined that this limited enforcement-discretion policy will discourage the continued, widespread use of certain research-use-only peptides supplied by foreign manufacturers that pose a safety risk to US patients" [1] [primary]. That is HHS's framing. The draft does not cover, authorise or legitimise RUO sales.

State-law note

The draft mentions States in its reporting condition and covers "State-licensed" pharmacies [1] [primary]. It contains no express statement about state pharmacy law. The law firm Frier Levitt writes that the policy "does not displace independent state pharmacy board requirements" and that pharmacies must still assess state law [7] [press]. That is the firm's analysis, not text from the policy. AJMC reports that Jeff Cohen, cofounder of the American Peptide Association, told Reuters that states may not follow the federal government in relaxing rules [11] [press]. That is a reported comment, not a statement of any state's position.

Petition and next PCAC review

On 23 Oct 2026 the Partnership for Safe Medicines (PSM) filed a citizen petition with FDA (docket FDA-2026-P-13366) [12] [primary, petitioner's filing]. It asks FDA to "refrain from taking action … to allow for compounding of drug products using any of the seven peptide bulk drug substances" considered at the 23–24 Jul 2026 PCAC meeting, and to "refrain from relying on" that meeting, which PSM says was constituted in violation of federal advisory-committee and ethics law [12]. PSM's press release describes this as urging FDA "to disregard the advisory committee vote that recommended allowing them" [13] [press release]. It is a petition to the agency, not a lawsuit, and no FDA response is reported in these sources.

AJMC reports that, as of July, the PCAC was scheduled to review five more unapproved peptides for pharmacy compounding in February [11] [press]. FDA's PCAC page says FDA "will host an advisory committee meeting before the end of February 2027" [14] [primary]. A scheduled review is not a listing.

Litigation context: Eli Lilly's retatrutide suits

On 12 Aug 2026, Eli Lilly announced six US lawsuits over unapproved retatrutide. Retatrutide is an investigational drug that Lilly says is in Phase 3 trials and not approved anywhere [8] [company-reported]. Lilly says the suits target "compounding pharmacies, medical spas, and online sellers that falsely claim their drugs are for 'research-use only' when they are actually intended for human use" [8] [company-reported]. The six cases it lists were filed in federal district courts in California and Texas [8] [company-reported]. Reuters reported the filings the same day [9] [press]. These are allegations, and no ruling is reported in these sources. Retatrutide is not one of the six peptides in the HHS draft.

FAQ

Did FDA approve these six peptides?

No. The notice comes from the HHS Office of the Secretary. It says compounded drugs are not FDA-approved, and none of the six is on the 503A Bulks List [1][2] [primary].

Is the policy final?

No. The Federal Register notice calls it a draft, says it is not binding, and opens a two-week comment window after publication on 30 Oct 2026 [2] [primary].

How long does it last?

No end date is given. It applies until a final rule addresses each substance, and HHS may revisit it at any time [1] [primary].

Does it cover blends such as BPC-157 with TB-500?

No. The draft requires a single listed active ingredient [1] [primary].

Does it cover RUO-labelled products?

No. Its terms depend on 503A compounding, a patient-specific prescription and registered CGMP sourcing. HHS calls foreign RUO peptides a safety risk [1] [primary].

Did FDA scientists support it?

Appendix B records that CDER recommended against listing each of the six and that the PCAC voted in favour [1] [primary].

peptide-legality-fda-ruo-compounding.html:
Last verified against FDA and HHS primary sources: 2026-10-31. Federal compounding lists, advisory votes, and enforcement priorities change. This guide is educational pathway literacy, not legal advice.

The short version

  1. FDA approval of a finished drug is not the same as pharmacy compounding permission, and neither is the same as an online “research use only” (RUO) listing.
  2. Under section 503A, a bulk drug substance generally may be used in compounding only if it has an applicable USP/NF monograph, is a component of an FDA-approved drug, or appears on the 503A Bulks List established by FDA rulemaking.
  3. While that Bulks List is developed, FDA has used interim categories. Category 1 is the interim bucket associated with practical enforcement discretion for compounding evaluation. Category 2 flags significant safety-risk concerns (do-not-compound posture under the interim policy framing).
  4. Removal from Category 2 is not permission to compound. It does not place a substance on the Bulks List and does not equal Category 1.
  5. A Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (PCAC) recommendation is advisory. It is not a final FDA rule and does not by itself authorize compounding.
  6. As of 29 October 2026, peptides reviewed at the July 2026 PCAC meeting (including BPC-157 and TB-500) had not been added to the 503A Bulks List by FDA rulemaking. The codified 503A Bulks List does not name them, and no proposed rule to add them has appeared in the Federal Register. Treat any “now legal to compound” claim with extreme skepticism unless it cites a final listing.
  7. On 28 October 2026 the HHS Office of the Secretary announced a draft interim policy, the “Enforcement Discretion Policy Regarding 503A Compounding Using Certain Peptide Bulk Drug Substances” (FR Doc. 2026-22192; Docket No. HHS-OASH-2026-0496). The notice of availability was published in the Federal Register on 30 October 2026 at 91 FR 68526, and Regulations.gov lists the comment period as closing on 13 November 2026. It describes when HHS does not intend to take enforcement action against certain 503A compounding of six peptides. It is not FDA approval of any peptide, not a 503A Bulks List listing, and not binding. See the dated update below.

Update, October 2026: draft interim enforcement-discretion policy (published for comment)

As of 31 October 2026. This section records a draft interim policy published for comment. It describes what the published text says. It is not legal advice, and it will be revised when the record changes. For how compounded drugs differ from RUO-labelled peptides under the draft, see Compounded vs RUO Peptides; for a summary of the six-peptide policy, see the HHS 503A explainer.

What the primary documents say

  • The notice. The HHS Office of the Secretary filed a Federal Register notice of availability, FR Doc. 2026-22192 (Docket No. HHS-OASH-2026-0496; RIN 0910-ZD94), on 28 October 2026. It was published in the Federal Register on 30 October 2026 as 91 FR 68526 (pages 68526–68527): https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/10/30/2026-22192/enforcement-discretion-policy-regarding-503a-compounding-using-certain-peptide-bulk-drug-substances . The notice states: “HHS is announcing the availability of a draft ‘Enforcement Discretion Policy Regarding 503A Compounding Using Certain Peptide Bulk Drug Substances.’” It describes “the Secretary of HHS’s enforcement policy regarding the use of certain peptide bulk drug substances in compounding pursuant to section 503A … while the list of bulk drug substances that can be used in compounding under section 503A of the FD&C Act (the 503A bulks list) is developed through rulemaking.”
  • Comment window. “Written comments can be submitted until 2 weeks after date of publication in the Federal Register via regulations.gov on Docket No. HHS-OASH-2026-0496.” The notice itself prints no calendar date. The Regulations.gov entry for the notice (HHS-OASH-2026-0496-0002) lists the comment period as closing on 13 November 2026 at 11:59 pm Eastern Time, two weeks after publication: https://www.regulations.gov/commenton/HHS-OASH-2026-0496-0002 .
  • OIRA review concluded. OIRA’s EO 12866 review of “Interim Access Policy for Compounding Using Certain Peptides” (RIN 0910-ZD94) shows Concluded Date: 10/27/2026 and Concluded Action: Consistent with Change.
  • Which peptides. Appendix A lists six: BPC-157, epitalon, KPV, MOTS-c, semax, and TB-500.
  • What HHS says it will do. “Until a peptide bulk drug substance is addressed in a final rule as being included or not included on the 503A bulks list, HHS does not intend to take action against a State licensed pharmacy, Federal facility, or licensed physician compounding a drug product using a peptide bulk drug substance that is not a component of an FDA-approved drug product, the subject of an applicable USP or NF monograph, or on the 503A bulks list codified at 21 CFR 216.23(a), when all of the following circumstances are present.”

Scope and conditions (as written; not usage guidance)

The policy lists ten conditions. In summary:

  • Listed identity and route only (Appendix B). BPC-157 acetate (subcutaneous, intramuscular, oral, and topical dosage forms); TB-500 acetate, the fragment Ac-Leu-Lys-Lys-Thr-Glu-Thr-Gln-OH (subcutaneous or intramuscular injectable dosage forms); MOTS-c acetate (subcutaneous or intramuscular injectable dosage forms); epitalon acetate (subcutaneous or intramuscular injectable dosage forms dispensed in intermittent courses); semax free base (intranasal use); KPV acetate (topical and oral dosage forms). Other salt forms are outside the listed identities. This list describes the policy’s scope. It is not usage guidance.
  • Sourcing and testing. The bulk substance must come from a facility registered under section 510 with a valid certificate of analysis, and the original manufacturer must be FDA-registered and CGMP-compliant, with its location listed on the certificate.
  • Reporting and labeling. Compounders report products compounded, serious adverse events, and product quality issues to FDA and to the States, and report serious adverse events and product quality issues to FDA’s MedWatch program. Labels must include “This is a compounded drug product. Not for resale.”
  • Single ingredient. “The compounded drug product contains only a single Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient (API) listed in Appendix A.” Blends are outside the policy.
  • Other limits. Oral forms need documentation of adequate oral bioavailability in humans; the only co-packaged device may be an FDA 510(k)-cleared syringe; and section 503A’s insanitary-conditions and patient-specific prescription requirements still apply.

What it is not

  • Not an FDA approval. The notice states: “Compounded drugs are not FDA-approved, which means FDA does not review their safety, effectiveness, or quality before they are marketed.” The documents make no safety or efficacy finding for any of the six peptides.
  • Not a 503A Bulks List listing. None of the six is on 21 CFR 216.23(a). The notice says “FDA’s future rulemakings may propose adding some or all of these peptides to the 503A bulks list”; that rulemaking is still pending.
  • Not Category 1. None of the six is in any FDA interim category. HHS’s Appendix B says each was in Category 2 until 22 April 2026, and FDA’s categories list updated 14 May 2026 does not name them.
  • Not binding and not permanent. The notice says the draft policy “does not establish any rights for any person and is not binding on HHS or the public.” There is no calendar end date: it runs until a final rule addresses each peptide, and “HHS may revisit application of this interim policy (in whole or in part) if, among other things, a safety signal or product quality issue arises.”
  • Not a change to RUO status. HHS states that the policy is meant to “discourage the continued, widespread use of certain research-use-only peptides supplied by foreign manufacturers that pose a safety risk to US patients.” Nothing in the policy treats research-use-only products as covered.
  • Advisory votes are still advisory. For each peptide, Appendix B states that FDA’s Center for Drug Evaluation and Research (CDER) recommended against listing and that the PCAC voted in favor. FDA has not posted vote results on its meeting page, and this guide gives no vote counts.

Petition, state law and the next PCAC meeting (as of 31 October 2026)

  • A citizen petition, not a lawsuit. On 23 October 2026 the Partnership for Safe Medicines (PSM) filed a citizen petition with FDA under 21 C.F.R. § 10.30 (Docket No. FDA-2026-P-13366). It asks FDA to “refrain from taking action, whether through regulation, addition to ‘Category 1’ … or otherwise through exercise of enforcement discretion or any other action, to allow for compounding of drug products using any of the seven peptide bulk drug substances” considered at the July 23–24, 2026 PCAC meeting. Because PSM argues that the July committee “was constituted in violation of the Federal Advisory Committee Act (‘FACA’) and the Ethics in Government Act (‘EIGA’)”, it also asks FDA to “refrain from relying on it”. PSM’s press release describes this as urging FDA “to disregard the advisory committee vote that recommended allowing them.” The petition was filed before HHS announced its policy. A citizen petition is a request to the agency. It is not litigation and not a ruling, and these sources report no FDA response. The FACA and ethics points are PSM’s arguments, not findings.
  • States may not follow. AJMC reports that Jeff Cohen, cofounder of the American Peptide Association, told Reuters that the move could heighten tension between federal and state regulators and that states may not follow the federal government in relaxing rules. That is a reported comment, not a legal conclusion. The HHS notice is a federal enforcement policy and does not itself state how any state will act.
  • Five more peptides at the next PCAC meeting (before the end of February 2027). AJMC reports that, as of July, the PCAC was scheduled to review five more unapproved peptides for pharmacy compounding in February. FDA’s PCAC meeting page says FDA “will host an advisory committee meeting before the end of February 2027” and lists five bulk drug substances (see the next-PCAC note below). A scheduled review is not a listing and not permission to compound.

Earlier reporting, and by whom

  • Washington Post, 7 October 2026. Rachel Roubein reported, citing two people familiar with the matter who spoke on condition of anonymity, that the administration was crafting plans to allow the temporary sale of certain previously restricted peptides through some compounding pharmacies while regulations are developed. That report predates the published text.
  • Holland & Knight, 16 October 2026. In a client alert written before the text was released, the law firm Holland & Knight (Sarah Starling Crossan and Shalyn Watkins) wrote that “the most likely approach of the policy is interim enforcement discretion.” This is one law firm’s analysis of a then-unpublished document, not HHS’s description of it.

The letter is signed by Jim Banks, Martin Heinrich, Ted Budd, Adam B. Schiff, Tom Cotton, Andy Kim, David H. McCormick, Jon Husted, and Todd Young. How 503A compounding lists actually work

Section 503A of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act governs traditional patient-specific compounding by state-licensed pharmacies (high level). FDA’s compounding pages explain that bulk drug substances used under 503A are limited. In plain language, a substance generally needs one of these pathways:

  • An applicable USP or NF monograph, or
  • Being a component of an FDA-approved drug, or
  • Appearing on FDA’s 503A Bulks List (built through agency evaluation / rulemaking)

Section 503B covers outsourcing facilities that register with FDA and face different bulk-substance and quality rules (including a separate 503B bulks / clinical-need framework and shortage-related pathways). This guide focuses on the 503A literacy most readers mean when they ask about “compounded peptides,” without turning into a full pharmacy-law manual.

Interim categories (why “Category 2” dominates headlines)

While formal bulks lists are developed, FDA has sorted nominated substances into interim categories. Educational explainers (including clinic/legal trackers) commonly describe:

  • Category 1 — substances under evaluation where FDA may exercise enforcement discretion; the only interim category that carries practical compounding consideration in that framing. Category 1 is still not FDA drug approval and is not, by itself, a license to compound.
  • Category 2 — substances FDA has identified as raising significant safety risks; do-not-compound posture under the interim policy
  • Category 3 — nominations lacking adequate supporting information (where that category is used)
  • Withdrawn nominations — a separate posture: nominators withdrew a nomination. Being “withdrawn” / off Category 2 is not permission

Two details from FDA’s 503A pages (503A page content current as of 14 May 2026) matter for the October 2026 news. First, FDA’s guidance “does not intend to place bulk drug substances nominated on or after January 7, 2025, into these categories.” Second, FDA’s 503A categories list, updated 14 May 2026, shows GHK-Cu (except for injectable routes of administration) added back to Category 1 after a nominator clarified its withdrawal. That is an interim enforcement-discretion posture with conditions, not FDA approval and not a Bulks List listing. Injectable GHK-Cu remains in the withdrawn-nomination table.

FDA also publishes a page on bulk substances that may present significant safety risks, including substances still listed under Category 2 and a table of substances whose nominations were withdrawn (with narrative safety concerns retained for context)—including entries such as BPC-157 and thymosin beta-4 fragment (LKKTETQ), also known as TB-500.

The distinction almost everyone gets wrong

In 2026, FDA actions that removed certain peptides from Category 2 (including via withdrawn nominations) were widely reported as those peptides “becoming legal again.” That is not what Category 2 removal means.

  • Off Category 2 ≠ on the 503A Bulks List
  • Off Category 2 ≠ Category 1
  • Off Category 2 ≠ automatic lawful compounding under 503A

A peptide can therefore be off Category 2 and still not lawfully compoundable under the interim framework—which is the situation many popular research peptides have been in while PCAC review and rulemaking continue.

What PCAC did—and did not do—in July 2026

On 23–24 July 2026, FDA’s Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee reviewed several nominated peptide bulk substances for possible 503A Bulks List inclusion. Reporting on the meeting (including BMJ coverage and legal analyses) describes committee votes that recommended inclusion for multiple peptides such as BPC-157 and TB-500, while FDA staff briefing materials had argued against inclusion for the set under review.

Critical literacy points:

  • PCAC votes are advisory and non-binding
  • FDA still decides whether/how to add a substance to the Bulks List
  • Addition generally requires notice-and-comment rulemaking
  • A favorable vote is not marketing approval as a drug
  • A favorable vote is not, by itself, a green light to compound

What “research use only” means—and does not

RUO / “not for human consumption” is a labeling and marketing posture. Legitimate laboratories do need research reagents. That is real.

What RUO does not automatically do:

  • Create FDA approval
  • Place a substance on a compounding bulks list
  • Guarantee purity, sterility, or correct identity
  • Erase FDA’s ability to evaluate intended use from the totality of marketing

Under 21 CFR 201.128, “intended uses” are based on objective intent—expressions, design/composition, and circumstances of distribution—including labeling claims and advertising. FDA warning letters to peptide sellers have treated website disease/structure-function style claims as evidence that products are being marketed as drugs, and then as unapproved new drugs when no approval is in effect—regardless of research branding.

The 24 August 2026 FDA warning letter to Peptide Partners LLC says this directly about that firm’s labeled products: despite statements marketing them “for research use only” and “not for human or veterinary use,” website evidence established that the products were intended to be drugs for human use. RUO wording on those products did not prevent the unapproved-new-drug finding in that letter. This is an enforcement example, not a complete list of every August 2026 letter and not legal advice about any other seller.

High-level takeaway: legality depends on pathway and marketing context, not on a disclaimer sticker. Static “legal or illegal” charts go stale quickly; prefer FDA primary pages and dated trackers over slogans.

WADA / sport (briefly)

Anti-doping rules are not general criminal law and are not FDA compounding law. Athletes subject to testing follow the WADA Prohibited List (and their sport’s program). As of the 2026 list:

  • BPC-157 — S0 (named example)
  • Thymosin-β4 and derivatives e.g. TB-500 — S2.3

A blend containing a prohibited substance is still a sport risk. Check the current list; it updates annually.

Practical literacy checklist (not legal advice)

  1. Is there an FDA-approved finished drug for this exact product/use?
  2. If compounded: does it qualify under 503A/503B pathways today (monograph, approved-drug component, or final bulks listing—not vibes)? Category 1 is interim enforcement discretion, not a qualifying pathway or a listing.
  3. Was a headline about Category 2 removal or a PCAC vote being treated as if it were a final rule?
  4. Is an online seller making drug claims while waving an RUO disclaimer?
  5. Do sport / DoD / employer rules separately restrict the substance?
  6. When in doubt: current FDA pages + qualified counsel—not forums.

FAQs

Are research peptides legal to buy online?

There is no single yes/no answer for every peptide, seller, claim, and jurisdiction. RUO listings exist; FDA still polices unapproved new drugs marketed for human use. This page does not advise purchases.

Does “removed from Category 2” mean pharmacies can compound it?

No. Removal from Category 2 is not placement on the 503A Bulks List and is not Category 1 permission.

Did PCAC “approve” BPC-157 or TB-500 in July 2026?

No. PCAC votes are non-binding recommendations. FDA’s briefing documents proposed that BPC-157 and TB-500 not be included, and the HHS policy’s Appendix B states that the committee voted in favor. A vote is not FDA drug approval and not a final bulks-list rule.

Did FDA approve compounded peptides in October 2026?

No. On 28 October 2026 the HHS Office of the Secretary announced a draft interim enforcement-discretion policy published for comment (FR Doc. 2026-22192). It describes when HHS does not intend to take action against certain 503A compounding of six peptides under listed conditions. It is not FDA drug approval, it does not place any peptide on the 503A Bulks List or in Category 1, it is not binding, and it makes no safety or efficacy finding. FDA rulemaking on the Bulks List is still pending.

Is compounding the same as FDA approval?

No. Compounding is a limited pharmacy pathway. Approval is a separate product authorization process.

Does WADA ban mean something is illegal for everyone?

No. WADA governs athletes in anti-doping programs. It is separate from FDA compounding and general consumer law—though the same substance can be constrained in multiple systems at once.

Where should I check status before believing a clinic ad?

FDA compounding / bulks / safety-risk pages first; then dated educational trackers; then counsel. On-site Peptidemap posts are context only—cross-check against primary FDA sources when making decisions.

What each is

BPC-157

BPC-157 (Body Protection Compound-157) is a synthetic 15-amino-acid peptide (a pentadecapeptide). It was first described in the early 1990s in work associated with researchers at the University of Zagreb and is often called a “stable gastric pentadecapeptide” because it was derived from a sequence related to human gastric juice and has been studied for stability in harsh gastrointestinal environments. It is also known in the literature under development names such as PL-14736, PLD-116, Bepecin, and PCO-02.

Neither the U.S. FDA nor other major drug regulators have approved BPC-157 as a medicine. A Phase 1 oral safety and pharmacokinetics trial (NCT02637284) was registered years ago. Its ClinicalTrials.gov status is listed as unknown, and it did not lead to an approved human use.

Thymosin beta-4 (Tβ4), the full-length protein

Thymosin beta-4 is an endogenous human protein encoded by the TMSB4X gene (UniProt P62328). The mature chain is 43 amino acids long, with an acetylated serine at its start, and it is present in many mammalian cells. PubChem lists it under the international nonproprietary name timbetasin (CID 16132341), with a molecular weight of about 4,963 g/mol. Researchers study it mainly for actin binding, cell migration, and wound repair.

Full-length Tβ4 is the molecule that drug developers have taken into human trials, mostly as eye drops (RGN-259) and topical gels for skin wounds. Those trials are described below. No Tβ4 product has reached FDA approval.

TB-500, the fragment sold under that name

“TB-500” is a marketplace name. For chemical identity, this page treats the U.S. FDA Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee briefing for 23–24 July 2026 as the source of record (FDA PCAC briefing, media/193349). That briefing describes TB-500 (free base) as “a seven amino acid synthetic fragment of thymosin beta-4 (β4) from amino acids 17 to 23,” with an N-terminal acetyl: Ac-Leu-Lys-Lys-Thr-Glu-Thr-Gln-OH (Ac-LKKTETQ). It also calls TB-500 “a synthetic N-acetylated heptapeptide containing the amino acid sequence 17 through 23 (LKKTETQ) of the full-length (43-amino acid) peptide thymosin β4,” and states that “thymosin beta-4 and TB-500 are not the same substance.” PubChem lists TB-500 as Ac-Leu-Lys-Lys-Thr-Glu-Thr-Gln-OH (CID 62707662), with a molecular weight of about 889 g/mol, roughly one-sixth the mass of full-length Tβ4.

Vendors sometimes blur the two labels. Some vendors use “TB-500” for the 17–23 fragment and others for full-length synthetic Tβ4, so the label alone does not show which molecule a vial contains. Neither is the trial material (such as RGN-259) tested in clinical studies. TB-500 is not an FDA-approved drug for injury recovery or any other indication.

Mechanisms (what researchers propose)

Mechanistic language below summarizes preclinical (mostly rodent and cell) findings. Proposed pathways do not prove that either peptide heals injuries in people.

BPC-157 — proposed pathways

Peer-reviewed reviews of the musculoskeletal literature describe multifactorial, “pleiotropic” signaling rather than a single receptor target. Commonly discussed themes in animal and in vitro work include:

  • Angiogenesis and growth signaling — upregulation of VEGF / VEGFR2-related pathways and other cell-growth cascades (for example ERK1/2, Akt)
  • Nitric oxide (NO) modulation — effects on NOS / eNOS-related pathways and vascular tone
  • Anti-inflammatory signaling — reduced markers such as COX-2 activity or cytokines (e.g., IL-6, TNF-α) in some models
  • Tendon fibroblast biology — increased migration, survival under stress, and growth-hormone receptor expression in cultured tendon cells
  • Tissue outcomes in animals — improved structural and functional measures after experimental muscle, tendon, ligament, and some bone injuries

A 2025 systematic review in HSS Journal (Vasireddi et al.) synthesized this literature for orthopaedic sports medicine and emphasized that almost all included outcome studies were preclinical.

Thymosin β4 and TB-500 — proposed pathways

Foundational reviews of thymosin β4 (including Goldstein, Hannappel & Kleinman, Trends in Molecular Medicine, 2005) describe it as a major actin-sequestering protein: it binds G-actin and supports cell motility, which is central to wound repair and tissue remodeling. Related preclinical themes include:

  • Cell migration and cytoskeletal reorganization
  • Angiogenesis and matrix remodeling in wound models
  • Broader repair biology across skin, cornea, and other tissues in animal work

A key distinction for readers: full-length Tβ4 biology is not automatically evidence for the TB-500 fragment. In FDA’s July 2026 briefing, TB-500 is a short synthetic piece of the parent molecule; vendor usage varies. A 2026 scoping review of 80 studies found that most work evaluated full-length Tβ4, and that direct TB-500 evidence was limited to a single study of metabolites and cultured fibroblasts. Mechanistic plausibility for actin-related repair does not equal proven efficacy of injectable TB-500 for human musculoskeletal injuries.

Complementary ≠ proven combination

Online stacking narratives often say BPC-157 is more “local / growth-factor oriented” and TB-500 more “systemic / cell-migration oriented.” That framing is a mechanistic hypothesis. It is not supported by combination trials in humans (see the Wolverine stack section below).

Animal vs human evidence limits

The evidence ladder, plainly

  1. Cell and animal studies can show biological activity and generate hypotheses.
  2. Human pharmacokinetics and safety trials test how a compound behaves in people.
  3. Randomized, controlled efficacy trials are what establish whether a treatment works for a defined condition.

For both marketplace peptides, especially for injectable use aimed at tendon, ligament, or muscle repair, the literature is heavily weighted toward step 1.

BPC-157 evidence status

Preclinical (stronger column): Multiple animal models report faster or better healing of experimental tendon transections, muscle injuries, ligament injuries, and related endpoints. Preclinical safety papers have reported no acute organ toxicity in animals, but that does not establish human safety for chronic or clinical use.

Human (much thinner): The Vasireddi et al. systematic review included 36 studies, 35 preclinical and 1 clinical. The clinical report was a small retrospective series of intra-articular BPC-157 for chronic knee pain without a control group, blinding, or standardized imaging endpoints. A 2026 systematic review in Acta Orthopaedica Belgica (Poolton et al.) searched to 1 June 2026 and found three human studies with 30 participants in total: a retrospective knee-injection series, a retrospective interstitial cystitis pilot, and a two-person intravenous safety pilot. It judged all three to be of poor methodological quality and rated the overall certainty of evidence very low. A narrative review (Current Reviews in Musculoskeletal Medicine, McGuire et al., 2025) similarly concludes that human data remain extremely limited.

Bottom line for BPC-157: Animal work is extensive relative to many research peptides. No randomized controlled human trial has shown that injectable BPC-157 heals sports injuries.

Full-length thymosin β4: what the human trials tested

Full-length Tβ4 has a real clinical-trial record, but almost all of it is on the surface of the eye or the skin, and the results are mixed.

  • Eye (RGN-259 eye drops). In a Phase 3 trial in neurotrophic keratopathy (SEER-1, NCT02600429; Sosne et al., Int J Mol Sci 2022), complete healing at four weeks occurred in 6 of 10 treated participants and 1 of 8 on placebo (p = 0.0656). The authors called this a trend; it did not reach the conventional significance threshold, and the trial ended early after 18 participants for a business decision. In dry eye, a 72-person Phase 2 trial (Sosne & Ousler, Clin Ophthalmol 2015) missed both primary endpoints, though some secondary endpoints favored Tβ4, and a 9-person Phase 2 trial in severe dry eye (Sosne et al., Cornea 2015) reported improvements in signs and symptoms. In the larger Phase 3 dry-eye trials ARISE-2 (NCT02974907, 601 enrolled) and ARISE-3 (NCT03937882, 700 enrolled), the results posted on ClinicalTrials.gov show primary-endpoint changes close to placebo. In ARISE-3, mean change in ocular discomfort at day 15 was −0.4 in both arms. A further neurotrophic keratopathy trial, SEER-2 (NCT05555589), is listed as recruiting.
  • Skin (topical Tβ4 gel, including RGN-137). A Phase 2 dose-escalation trial in venous stasis ulcers randomized 73 patients at eight European sites (Guarnera et al., Ann N Y Acad Sci 2010). It reported a safety profile comparable to placebo, and its efficacy findings were exploratory. A pressure-ulcer Phase 2 trial (NCT00382174) enrolled 72 patients. Two epidermolysis bullosa trials stopped early: NCT00311766 for lack of patient availability and expiration of study drug, and the RGN-137 trial NCT03578029 after enrolling 4 participants, for a business decision.
  • Injected recombinant Tβ4. Two Phase 2 trials after heart attack have been run in China (NCT05485818 and NCT05984134). ClinicalTrials.gov lists both as completed, with no posted results.

The 2026 scoping review by McGuire, Hughes, Maak, and Cushman (Applied Sciences) found human Tβ4 evidence concentrated in eye and skin settings and identified no human interventional studies of administered Tβ4 or TB-500 in tendon, ligament, muscle, bone, cartilage, or spine.

TB-500 evidence status

Preclinical: Direct TB-500 research is thin. The scoping review above found one direct TB-500 study, on metabolites and cultured fibroblasts. A 2026 rat Achilles study used material its authors called “synthetic thymosin beta-4 (TB-500)” (see the Wolverine stack section).

Human: No published human study of TB-500 was identified. FDA’s July 2026 PCAC briefing states: “The nomination did not include, and FDA has not identified, any clinical studies or human exposure data using TB-500 via any ROA. Therefore, potential safety risks associated with the use of TB-500 in humans are unknown.” (ROA means route of administration.) The same briefing says that “no articles were found in which TB-500 was administered to humans.” One Phase 1/2 safety trial of “TB-500 (Thymosin Beta 4 17-23 Fragment)” in adults with stable atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (TBRIDGE-CV, NCT07487363) was first posted on ClinicalTrials.gov on 23 March 2026. It is listed as recruiting, with an estimated 80 participants and no results posted.

Bottom line for TB-500: Do not read Tβ4 eye-drop or skin-gel trials as evidence that injected TB-500 repairs musculoskeletal injuries in people. They tested a different, much larger molecule by a different route.

What absence of evidence means (and does not mean)

Missing human RCTs does not prove these peptides “don’t work.” It also does not prove they do. It means anyone claiming settled human efficacy, or settled human safety, for injectable injury use is saying more than the published record supports.

The “Wolverine stack” nickname: what was and was not studied

“Wolverine stack” is a nickname that vendors and online communities use for pairing BPC-157 with TB-500, often sold as a pre-mixed blend. A pre-mixed blend still contains two separate peptides; it is not one molecule. It is a marketing and community label. It is not a trial name, a regulatory category, or a protocol. Common justifications for the pairing are:

  • Different proposed mechanisms might be complementary
  • Testimonials from clinics or forums, which are not controlled evidence
  • Marketing convenience (one vial instead of two)

What is actually published about combining them?

No human trial has studied BPC-157 and TB-500 together. We did not identify peer-reviewed human studies that prospectively test co-administration for safety, pharmacokinetics, interactions, or musculoskeletal efficacy.

One retrospective clinic chart review of knee injections (Lee & Padgett, Altern Ther Health Med 2021; PMID 34324435) included 4 patients who received BPC-157 with thymosin β4. It had no control group and did not identify the thymosin β4 material, so it is not a trial of the pair.

One animal study is on the record. Biçer and colleagues compared BPC-157, TB-500, and the combination in a rat Achilles tendon healing model (histopathology and biomechanics): Biçer O, et al. Jt Dis Relat Surg 2026;37(3):822–837 (full text; DOI 10.52312/jdrs.2026.2951; PMID 42542926). The abstract states: “Combined BPC-157 and TB-500 treatment did not confer additional benefits compared to either agent alone.” Its results paragraph covers maximum load to failure, total Bonar score, and total Movin score. The discussion states that the combination “did not demonstrate superior biomechanical or histopathological outcomes compared to monotherapy.”

This is a rat study, not a human trial. It is not a protocol, and it is not a reason to combine the two. The paper calls its material “synthetic thymosin beta-4 (TB-500).” It was not confirmed that the vial was the 7-residue Ac-LKKTETQ fragment rather than full-length thymosin β4, so do not read the rat result as a test of the FDA briefing’s heptapeptide specifically. Blend calculators and timing schedules circulating online are not derived from clinical trials of the pair.

A July 2026 advisory committee vote does not change this picture. The PCAC voted on each substance separately, not on the pair, and a committee vote is not an FDA approval (see below).

Educational takeaway: Treat “Wolverine stack” claims as untested hypotheses, not as evidence-based regimens. This page intentionally does not provide combination ratios, schedules, or administration guidance.

FDA / sport context

Regulatory status changes; verify current primary sources before relying on any summary, including this one.

FDA: not approved drugs; compounding is a separate question

  • Neither BPC-157 nor TB-500 is an FDA-approved drug for any indication.
  • FDA’s page “Certain Bulk Drug Substances for Use in Compounding that May Present Significant Safety Risks” (content current as of 22 April 2026) lists BPC-157 and “Thymosin beta-4, fragment (LKKTETQ), also known as TB-500” in its table “Bulk drug substances nominated but withdrawn”, which FDA describes as substances previously in category 2 of its interim policies that the nominators withdrew. For BPC-157 it describes immunogenicity risk for some routes, peptide impurity and API characterization complexity, and “no, or only limited, safety-related information for the proposed routes of administration.” For TB-500 it states, in FDA’s wording: “FDA has not identified any human exposure data drug products containing Thymosin Beta-4, Fragment. FDA lacks important information regarding any safety issues raised by this drug, including whether it would cause harm if administered to humans.”
  • For the 23–24 July 2026 Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (PCAC) meeting, FDA staff reviewed TB-500 for the section 503A Bulks List for the nominated use of wound healing and concluded: “we propose not adding TB-500 (free base) or TB-500 acetate to the 503A Bulks List.”
  • The committee voted the other way. The BMJ reported on 28 July 2026 that PCAC recommended six peptides, including BPC-157 and TB-500, each by a narrow majority; the one peptide it did not recommend was emideltide (DSIP). FDA staff had proposed against BPC-157 as well: its separate briefing concluded, “we propose not adding BPC-157 (free base) or BPC-157 acetate to the 503A Bulks List” (FDA PCAC briefing, media/193343, PDF p. 47). PCAC votes are advisory and non-binding. FDA’s briefing states that it “will not issue a final determination on the issues at hand until input from the advisory committee process has been considered and all reviews have been finalized.” A favorable vote is not FDA final listing, not marketing approval, and not lawful compounding authority by itself.

“Research use only” labeling on online vials does not create a legal pathway for human treatment and does not substitute for pharmaceutical quality systems. For pathway literacy (Category 2 removal is not Category 1 and is not the 503A Bulks List), see Are research peptides legal? FDA, RUO, and compounding.

Department of Defense / service members

The DoD Operation Supplement Safety (OPSS) program describes BPC-157 as an unapproved drug and lists it among prohibited dietary supplement ingredients for service members. OPSS notes that marketed benefits have been shown mainly in lab or animal studies and that well-designed human evidence for safety and effectiveness is lacking.

Sport / WADA

Under the WADA 2026 Prohibited List (effective 1 January 2026):

  • BPC-157 is named under S0 Non-approved substances (prohibited at all times).
  • Thymosin-β4 and its derivatives, e.g. TB-500, are named under S2.3 Growth factors and growth factor modulators (prohibited at all times). That entry covers full-length Tβ4 as well as the fragment.

Athletes in tested sports should treat products containing either peptide, including blends, as a doping risk regardless of intent or “research chemical” labeling. Individual leagues may have additional policies.

FAQs

Are BPC-157 and TB-500 the same peptide?

No. BPC-157 is a synthetic 15-amino-acid peptide from the gastric-cytoprotection research line. TB-500 usually refers to a short synthetic fragment of thymosin beta-4, a different endogenous protein involved in actin binding and cell migration. They are chemically unrelated.

Is TB-500 the same as thymosin beta-4?

No. Full-length thymosin beta-4 is a 43-amino-acid human protein. In FDA’s July 2026 briefing, TB-500 is a 7-amino-acid acetylated fragment, Ac-LKKTETQ, which matches residues 17 to 23 of thymosin beta-4; vendors do not always use the name this way. The same briefing states that “thymosin beta-4 and TB-500 are not the same substance.” Full-length thymosin beta-4 has been tested in human trials as eye drops and skin gels, with mixed results. No published human study of TB-500 was identified.

Is either one FDA-approved for healing injuries?

No. Neither is an FDA-approved drug for musculoskeletal healing or any other indication. Compounding-list discussions, including PCAC recommendations, are not the same as drug approval.

Does animal evidence mean they work in humans?

No. Animal and cell studies can be scientifically interesting and still fail to predict human outcomes. For injectable injury recovery claims, neither peptide has randomized controlled human trial evidence.

What is the “Wolverine stack”?

It is a nickname that vendors and online communities use for pairing BPC-157 with TB-500. It is not a trial name or a protocol. No human trial has studied the pair. A 2026 rat Achilles study (Biçer et al., Jt Dis Relat Surg) reported that combined BPC-157 and TB-500 did not confer additional benefits compared with either agent alone, and that paper did not confirm its “TB-500” was the Ac-LKKTETQ fragment. A July 2026 FDA advisory committee vote recommending each substance for the 503A bulks list is advisory and is not FDA approval. Peptidemap does not give dosing or combination instructions.

Are these substances banned in sport?

Yes under WADA rules as of the 2026 Prohibited List: BPC-157 is named in S0; thymosin-β4 and derivatives including TB-500 are named in S2.3. Both classes are prohibited at all times. Check your sport’s governing body as well.

Why do so many sites recommend them together?

They are marketed together, share overlapping online recovery audiences, and have complementary-sounding proposed mechanisms. Marketing frequency is not the same as clinical validation.

Retatrutide is an investigational once-weekly injection that acts on GIP, GLP-1 and glucagon receptors. It is not approved anywhere. This article collects the adverse events reported in the primary trial publications, the ClinicalTrials.gov results that have been posted, and, where no full paper was available, figures Lilly has released. Each number is labelled with where it came from. Nothing here is a dosing guide, a safety verdict or medical advice.

How to read the numbers on this page

The trials tested several dose arms. This article names them by position only: the lowest dose arm, the middle dose arm and the highest dose arm, plus placebo. The two phase 2 trials had more arms than that, including pairs of arms that reached the same dose from a lower or a higher starting dose. For those trials the tables show the lowest dose arm, the highest dose arm, and the range across every retatrutide arm. These positions are relative to each trial's own arms: the lowest, middle or highest dose arm in one trial is not necessarily the same dose as the arm in the same position in another trial.

Three kinds of source appear below:

  • Paper: the peer-reviewed publication. For the two phase 2 trials, the full text was read. For TRIUMPH-2, the rows labelled Paper are those in the published paper. TRIUMPH-1 figures that appear in the NEJM paper are labelled as reported in the paper and company-reported by Lilly.
  • Registry: results posted on ClinicalTrials.gov. These use the trial's own adverse-event terms and time frames, which can differ from the paper's.
  • Company-reported: figures from Lilly press releases or Lilly Medical Information pages. These have not been peer reviewed, and they are labelled as company-reported every time they appear.

Percentages are the share of participants with at least one event, unless stated otherwise. Phase 2, TRIUMPH-1 and TRIUMPH-2 paper figures use the safety population, meaning participants who received at least one dose, except the TRIUMPH-1 discontinuation figures, which Table 3 of the NEJM paper reports against the randomized population. The TRIUMPH-1 and TRIUMPH-2 papers were funded by Lilly and include Lilly-employed authors (developer-affiliated). Lilly's releases do not define their analysis set. These are safety counts, not efficacy results, so the efficacy and treatment-regimen estimands used for weight outcomes do not apply to them. Rates from different trials are not directly comparable. The populations, durations, escalation schemes and event definitions differ. The trial details sit on the retatrutide encyclopedia entry.   • Phase 2 type 2 diabetes. 16 of 190 retatrutide participants (8%) discontinued, most often for gastrointestinal events (6, or 3%). The highest arm-level rate, 17%, was in an intermediate-dose arm with fast escalation.
  • TRIUMPH-1. The figures are from Table 3 of the NEJM paper, whose footnote says these events exclude deaths and use the randomized population as the denominator. The paper's results text and participant-flow figure give 11.1% for the highest dose arm. Both describe the same 65 participants: 65 of the 584 randomized to that arm is 11.1%, while Table 3 prints 11.2%, which matches 65 of the 582 in that arm who received at least one dose.
  • TRIUMPH-2. The middle dose arm had a higher rate than the highest dose arm, in both the paper's counts and the company's percentages. Neither source accessible here explains why.
  • TRIUMPH-4. Lilly said discontinuations were "highly correlated with baseline BMI" and "included discontinuations for perceived excessive weight loss". In participants with a baseline BMI of 35 or higher, the company-reported rates were 4.8% with placebo and 8.8% and 12.1% in the two retatrutide arms.

The ClinicalTrials.gov participant-flow tables list a separate figure: withdrawals from the study recorded as "Adverse Event". These are not the same as stopping study drug and are smaller numbers. They should not be read as discontinuation rates.

Heart rate and its time course

Both phase 2 papers describe a rise in heart rate that peaked and then fell during treatment.

  • Phase 2 obesity (paper). Heart rate "increased in a dose-dependent manner with retatrutide up to 24 weeks and then declined thereafter". The discussion describes the increase as peaking at 24 weeks, followed by a decline at 36 and 48 weeks. The numeric changes are in the supplementary appendix, which was not reviewed for this article, so no values are given here.
  • Phase 2 type 2 diabetes (paper). Pulse rose by "up to approximately 7 bpm" early in treatment and had decreased by 36 weeks. At 36 weeks the mean change ranged from 0.03 to 4.34 beats per minute across the retatrutide arms. It was minus 3.16 with placebo and 1.76 with dulaglutide. The paper says the week-36 retatrutide changes were not significantly different from dulaglutide. They were significantly different from placebo in every retatrutide arm except one escalation arm (p=0.0819).
  • TRIUMPH-1 (paper). The NEJM paper reports that mean pulse rate increased with retatrutide, peaked at 20 weeks in the middle and highest dose arms and decreased thereafter (appendix Figure S22). At week 80 the change from baseline was 1.5, 2.7 and 2.6 beats per minute in the lowest, middle and highest dose arms vs −0.3 with placebo (appendix Table S12, model-based estimates, safety population). Heart-rate time courses for TRIUMPH-2, TRIUMPH-3 and TRIUMPH-4 are not covered here.

Dysesthesia, allodynia and skin-sensation events

Different trials used different terms for these events. They should not be pooled as if they were one measure.

What the phase 2 trials reported

The phase 2 obesity paper grouped events as "hyperesthesia or related". These occurred in 1% with placebo, 1% in the lowest dose arm and 13% in the highest dose arm, with a range of 1% to 14% across the retatrutide arms. The text says "cutaneous hyperesthesia and skin sensitivity adverse events were reported in 7% of the participants who received retatrutide and 1% of those who received placebo." It adds that none were severe or serious, none were associated with overt skin findings, and none led to discontinuation. The discussion says the events "did not appear to be related to the magnitude or rate of weight loss".

The posted ClinicalTrials.gov results for the same trial list three separate terms:

  • Allodynia: 4 of 62 participants in the highest dose arm, and none in any other arm or with placebo.
  • Hyperaesthesia: 1 participant on placebo, and reported in five of the six retatrutide arms.
  • Sensitive skin: reported in three of the retatrutide arms and not with placebo.

In the phase 2 type 2 diabetes paper, "hyperaesthesia and related adverse events" occurred in 3 of 281 participants (1%): none with placebo or in the lowest dose arm, and 1 participant (2%) in the highest dose arm.

What the TRIUMPH program reported

The phase 3 trials report dysesthesia. Lilly's Medical Information page defines it as "a skin burning sensation and related adverse events" and says events were mostly mild to moderate.

What has not been characterized in these sources

  • Mechanism. None of the sources reviewed establish why these events occur.
  • Onset and duration. The sources give no time to onset or duration, and no breakdown of how many events resolved. Lilly's TRIUMPH-1 and TRIUMPH-2/3 releases say dysesthesia events (reported together with urinary tract infections) were generally mild to moderate and that the majority resolved during treatment, without counts or timing.
  • Clinical workup. No neurological examination, nerve-conduction or skin-biopsy findings for the phase 3 trials appear in the sources reviewed.
  • Terminology. No source reviewed explains whether the phase 2 "hyperesthesia or related" cluster and the phase 3 "dysesthesia" definition cover the same preferred terms. Allodynia appears as a separate term only in the phase 2 obesity registry results.
  • Weight loss. The phase 2 obesity statement that the events did not track the magnitude or rate of weight loss has not been repeated for phase 3 in the sources reviewed.

Arrhythmia, hepatobiliary, pancreatitis and hypoglycaemia findings

These are reported only where a source gives them.

Arrhythmia and cardiovascular events

  • Phase 2 obesity (paper). Cardiac arrhythmias, meaning supraventricular arrhythmias and conduction disorders, occurred in 3% with placebo, 4% in the lowest dose arm and 11% in the highest dose arm. The range across the retatrutide arms was 0 to 14%. The paper says these events were mild to moderate, except one severe prolonged QT in a participant treated with ondansetron.
  • Phase 2 type 2 diabetes (paper). The same category occurred in 14 of 281 participants (5%): 2% with placebo, 4% in the lowest dose arm and 7% in the highest dose arm. The registry lists one serious atrial fibrillation event in a retatrutide arm.

The TRIUMPH-1 and TRIUMPH-2 papers (Table 3 in each) report counts of participants with severe or serious arrhythmias and cardiac conduction disorders. Lilly Medical Information reports the same counts (company-reported).

TRIUMPH-3 (company-reported). This trial enrolled people with established cardiovascular disease. Lilly reported 44 vs 52 five-component MACE events (hazard ratio 0.82, 95% CI 0.55 to 1.22) and 27 vs 23 three-component MACE events (hazard ratio 1.12, 95% CI 0.64 to 1.96), retatrutide vs placebo (pre-specified in-study analysis). Lilly says MACE occurred less often than anticipated in both arms. Both confidence intervals cross 1, and these figures do not establish a cardiovascular benefit or harm. Liver and gallbladder

  • Phase 2 obesity (paper). Transient rises in ALT to more than 3 times the upper limit of normal occurred in 1% of retatrutide recipients. Mean ALT and AST were unchanged or lower at week 48. Biliary events occurred in 3 participants, all on retatrutide: 1 cholecystitis and 2 cholelithiasis.
  • Phase 2 type 2 diabetes (paper). Hepatic or biliary disorders occurred in 4 of 281 participants (1%), including 1 on placebo. Mean ALT and AST generally decreased. The investigator attributed one serious cholecystitis to study drug.
  • TRIUMPH-2 (paper). The Lancet paper (Table 3) reports severe or serious gallbladder and biliary tract disorders in 3, 1 and 1 participants in the lowest, middle and highest dose arms vs 1 with placebo, and severe or serious hepatic disorders in 1, 0 and 0 vs 1. Lilly Medical Information lists the same counts (company-reported).
  • TRIUMPH-1 (paper). Table 3 of the NEJM paper reports severe or serious gallbladder or biliary tract disorders in 10, 5 and 4 participants in the lowest, middle and highest dose arms vs 4 with placebo, and severe or serious hepatic disorders in 0, 0 and 3 vs 0. Hepatobiliary counts for TRIUMPH-3 and TRIUMPH-4 were not in the sources reviewed.

Pancreatitis

  • Phase 2 obesity (paper). One adjudicated case of acute pancreatitis, in the highest dose arm, was reported as a serious adverse event. Otherwise, amylase and lipase increases were asymptomatic.
  • Phase 2 type 2 diabetes (paper). Two adjudicated pancreatitis events occurred, one in the lowest dose arm and one in a middle dose arm (one of the four arms between the lowest and highest). The investigator attributed one of them to study drug: it occurred 7 days after that participant's only dose.
  • TRIUMPH-2 (paper). The Lancet paper (Table 3) reports adjudication-confirmed pancreatitis in 0, 1 and 2 participants in the lowest, middle and highest dose arms vs 0 with placebo. Lilly Medical Information lists the same counts (company-reported).
  • TRIUMPH-1 (paper). Table 3 of the NEJM paper reports adjudication-confirmed pancreatitis in 1, 3 and 4 participants in the lowest, middle and highest dose arms vs 2 with placebo. Pancreatitis counts for TRIUMPH-3 and TRIUMPH-4 were not in the sources reviewed.

Hypoglycaemia

  • Phase 2 obesity (paper). No clinically significant hypoglycaemia was reported.
  • Phase 2 type 2 diabetes (paper). No severe hypoglycaemia was reported. Hypoglycaemia below 54 mg/dL occurred in one participant in each of three retatrutide arms, including the highest dose arm, and in no one on placebo.
  • TRIUMPH-2 (paper). The Lancet paper (Table 3) reports level 2 or level 3 hypoglycaemia in 2, 4 and 9 participants in the lowest, middle and highest dose arms vs 5 with placebo. Lilly Medical Information lists the same counts (company-reported).

Serious adverse events and deaths

  • Phase 2 obesity (paper). Serious adverse events occurred in 4% of both the retatrutide and placebo groups. One death, by drowning, was assessed by the investigator as not related to retatrutide.
  • Phase 2 type 2 diabetes (paper). There were no deaths. The investigator attributed three serious adverse events to study drug: cholecystitis, acute pancreatitis and starvation ketoacidosis.
  • TRIUMPH-2 (paper). There were 2, 3 and 1 deaths in the lowest, middle and highest dose arms and 1 with placebo, all deemed unrelated by the investigator. The authors describe the safety profile as "generally consistent with other molecules with GLP-1 receptor agonism".

What the trials can't tell us

  • Duration. Treatment lasted 36 to 80 weeks. Events that take longer to appear, or that depend on years of exposure, are outside what these trials could detect.
  • Populations. Both phase 2 trials ran at US sites only. The trials enrolled specific groups: people without diabetes, people with type 2 diabetes, people with cardiovascular disease and people with knee osteoarthritis. They screened out people with many other conditions. Results in one group do not automatically carry over to another.
  • Rare events. Single-digit counts of pancreatitis, gallbladder or arrhythmia events cannot produce precise rates. TRIUMPH-1 (NEJM) and TRIUMPH-2 (Lancet) publish arm-level counts for these events; other TRIUMPH readouts remain company-reported.
  • Full phase 3 data. Arm-level phase 3 heart-rate data were found only for TRIUMPH-1 (appendix Table S12 and Figure S22), and the time course of dysesthesia was not available in the sources reviewed. For hepatobiliary events and pancreatitis, the arm-level phase 3 figures used here are TRIUMPH-1 counts from Table 3 of the NEJM paper and TRIUMPH-2 counts from the Lancet paper, which Lilly Medical Information also lists. For hypoglycaemia, the arm-level phase 3 figures used here are TRIUMPH-2 counts from the Lancet paper, which Lilly Medical Information also lists. TRIUMPH-1 (NEJM) and TRIUMPH-2 (Lancet) are published papers; other TRIUMPH readouts used above remain company-reported.
  • Monitored conditions. Trial participants received pharmaceutical-grade study drug under a protocol, with set escalation steps, scheduled visits, laboratory monitoring and adjudication of key events. Those conditions are part of what the numbers describe.

Research-labelled "retatrutide" is not the trial drug

Retatrutide is not approved by the FDA or any other regulator. Lilly states that it "cannot be legally sold or marketed for human use" and is legally available only to participants in its clinical trials. Vials sold online as research-use-only "retatrutide" are not the trial material. Their identity, purity, sterility and contents are not covered by any of the data above, and their use is not monitored. The trial adverse-event rates do not describe what happens with those products. The peptide legality guide explains what research-use-only labelling does and does not mean. A separate article covers what retatrutide testing and COAs can and cannot show.

FAQ

What were the most common side effects in the retatrutide trials?

Gastrointestinal events: nausea, diarrhoea, vomiting, constipation and decreased appetite. In both phase 2 papers they were dose-related and mostly mild to moderate, and the obesity paper says they occurred mainly during dose escalation. In the TRIUMPH-2 paper, diarrhoea was reported in 27% to 34% of the retatrutide arms vs 13% with placebo, and nausea in 14% to 28% vs 8%.

How many people stopped retatrutide because of adverse events?

In the phase 2 obesity trial, 6% to 16% of the retatrutide arms vs none on placebo. In the phase 2 type 2 diabetes trial, 16 of 190 retatrutide participants (8%) vs 2 of 45 on placebo (4%). In the TRIUMPH-2 paper, permanent discontinuation due to adverse events or death was 4%, 12% and 8% in the lowest, middle and highest dose arms vs 5% with placebo. In the TRIUMPH-1 paper, discontinuation of study drug due to adverse events (randomized population, excluding deaths) was 4.1%, 6.5% and 11.2% in the lowest, middle and highest dose arms vs 4.6% with placebo.

Does retatrutide raise heart rate?

In the phase 2 obesity paper, heart rate rose in a dose-dependent manner, peaked at 24 weeks and declined at 36 and 48 weeks. In the phase 2 type 2 diabetes paper, pulse rose by up to about 7 beats per minute early in treatment and had decreased by 36 weeks. The TRIUMPH-1 NEJM paper reports that mean pulse rate peaked at 20 weeks in the middle and highest dose arms and then decreased (appendix Figure S22); at week 80 the change from baseline was 1.5, 2.7 and 2.6 beats per minute in the lowest, middle and highest dose arms vs −0.3 with placebo (appendix Table S12).

What is the dysesthesia reported in the TRIUMPH trials?

Lilly defines it as a skin burning sensation and related adverse events. In the TRIUMPH-2 paper it was reported in 4% to 7% of the retatrutide arms vs 1% with placebo. The TRIUMPH-1 rate of up to 12.5% is reported in the paper and company-reported by Lilly. Company-reported rates were up to 20.9% in TRIUMPH-4. Lilly says events were generally mild to moderate and most resolved during treatment. The cause, timing and duration have not been characterized in the sources reviewed.

Were pancreatitis, gallbladder or hypoglycaemia events reported?

In the phase 2 papers these events were few. The obesity trial reported one acute pancreatitis, three biliary events and no clinically significant hypoglycaemia. The type 2 diabetes trial reported two adjudicated pancreatitis events and three participants with hypoglycaemia below 54 mg/dL, none severe. In the TRIUMPH-1 paper, Table 3 reports severe or serious gallbladder or biliary tract disorders in 10, 5 and 4 participants in the lowest, middle and highest dose arms vs 4 with placebo, severe or serious hepatic disorders in 0, 0 and 3 vs 0, and adjudication-confirmed pancreatitis in 1, 3 and 4 vs 2. That table does not report hypoglycaemia. In the TRIUMPH-2 paper, Table 3 reports severe or serious gallbladder and biliary tract disorders in 3, 1 and 1 vs 1 with placebo, severe or serious hepatic disorders in 1, 0 and 0 vs 1, adjudication-confirmed pancreatitis in 0, 1 and 2 vs 0, and level 2 or level 3 hypoglycaemia in 2, 4 and 9 vs 5.

Is research-labelled retatrutide the same as the trial drug?

No. Retatrutide is investigational and not approved anywhere. Lilly states it cannot be legally sold or marketed for human use. Products sold online as research-labelled retatrutide are not the material used in these trials, and the trial safety data do not describe them.

Can these trials be compared with trials of other drugs?

Not reliably. The trials differ in population, duration, dose escalation and how events were defined and counted. This article reports results within each trial only and does not rank retatrutide against other drugs.

Retatrutide and semaglutide both act on the GLP-1 receptor, but they are at very different stages. Retatrutide, from Eli Lilly, is an investigational once-weekly injection that also acts on GIP and glucagon receptors. As of 28 October 2026, one head-to-head Phase 3 trial of the two, TRANSCEND-T2D-2 in type 2 diabetes, has company-reported topline results that are not yet peer-reviewed or published.

This article covers what each molecule is, how their mechanisms differ, what each trial program measured, the side effects reported in the trial publications, and where each stands with regulators. Retatrutide and semaglutide figures are kept in separate tables, because they come from different trials with different populations, durations and analysis methods.

Retatrutide. The TRIUMPH-1 paper in the New England Journal of Medicine describes retatrutide as "a triple-receptor agonist of glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide, glucagon-like peptide-1, and glucagon receptors." The 2023 phase 2 obesity paper calls it "a single peptide conjugated to a fatty diacid moiety" and reports a half-life of about 6 days, which allows weekly injection. An FDA letter dated 2 October 2026 describes it as a chain of 39 alpha amino acids with a side chain that includes a C20 fatty diacid.

Semaglutide. The current Wegovy prescribing information (NDA 215256/S-031, approved 5 May 2026) describes semaglutide as "a GLP-1 analogue with 94% sequence homology to human GLP-1" that "selectively binds to and activates the GLP-1 receptor." Its peptide backbone is made by yeast fermentation. It is modified to resist breakdown by the DPP-4 enzyme and carries a C18 fatty diacid that binds albumin. Per the label, its elimination half-life is about 1 week. The same molecule is sold under several brand names, and each product has its own approved uses.

Peptidemap's compound pages are Retatrutide and Semaglutide.

Mechanism: triple agonist vs GLP-1 receptor agonist

Both molecules activate the GLP-1 receptor. The Wegovy label calls GLP-1 "a physiological regulator of appetite and caloric intake" and notes that the receptor is present in brain areas involved in appetite regulation.

Retatrutide adds two more targets:

  • GIP receptor. GIP is a second gut hormone released after meals. In laboratory assays cited in the phase 2 obesity paper, retatrutide was more potent than natural GIP at the human GIP receptor.
  • Glucagon receptor. Glucagon is a pancreatic hormone. The phase 2 authors write that adding glucagon receptor agonism "may further reduce energy intake, increase energy expenditure, or both." They describe this as a premise and a speculation, not an established human mechanism.

The same paper reports that, compared with the natural hormones, retatrutide is less potent at the human glucagon and GLP-1 receptors. A triple-receptor design is a difference in pharmacology. On its own, it says nothing about whether a drug is more effective or safer. One head-to-head Phase 3 trial in type 2 diabetes, TRANSCEND-T2D-2, has company-reported topline results as of 28 Oct 2026 that are not yet peer-reviewed or published.

Has there been a head-to-head trial?

TRANSCEND-T2D-2: topline results (company-reported, 28 Oct 2026)

On 28 Oct 2026, Eli Lilly announced topline results from TRANSCEND-T2D-2, the first Phase 3 trial comparing retatrutide with another incretin medicine [23][24] [company-reported]. The trial was randomised and open-label. It compared two once-weekly retatrutide dose arms (the middle and highest of the three retatrutide dose levels used in the TRIUMPH trials) with once-weekly injectable semaglutide (Ozempic) in 1,298 adults with type 2 diabetes not controlled on metformin, with or without an SGLT2 inhibitor [23]. Its registry record is NCT06260722 [7]. Lilly says it chose the semaglutide arm because it was "the highest approved dose" [23] [company-reported].

The primary objective was noninferiority on A1C change at 80 weeks for the highest dose arm versus semaglutide. Body-weight change was a key secondary endpoint [23]. Lilly reported that retatrutide "met the primary and all key secondary endpoints" [23] [company-reported]. All figures Lilly released use the efficacy estimand, which estimates results had all participants stayed on treatment without added glucose-lowering medicine [23]. This page does not reproduce per-arm figures.

Lilly said gastrointestinal events were the most common adverse events and that dysesthesia was also reported [23] [company-reported].

This is a topline company announcement. It has not been peer-reviewed, and full results are not yet published. Lilly says detailed results will be presented at a medical meeting and published in a journal [23]. Retatrutide is investigational and is not approved anywhere [23].

A semaglutide arm, open-label, is included as a secondary comparison. The study is active, not recruiting, with completion estimated for January 2027.
