Regulatory status

Retatrutide: investigational, not approved by the FDA or the EMA.

  • A search of FDA drug-approval records (openFDA Drugs@FDA data, 19 October 2026) found no retatrutide product. EMA's published list of medicines (downloaded 19 October 2026) includes no retatrutide entry.
  • 23 July 2026: Lilly said it is completing the chemistry, manufacturing and controls package and plans to submit retatrutide for US approval in the first quarter of 2027, as a Biologics License Application (company-reported). A planned submission is not an approval.
  • The FDA has twice concluded (March 2024 and October 2026) that retatrutide is a drug, not a biological product. A federal court sent the first decision back to the agency in October 2025, and Lilly's appeal is pending at the Seventh Circuit with no ruling as of 19 October 2026. For general background on FDA status and RUO labelling, see our legality guide.
  • Lilly states that retatrutide "cannot be legally sold or marketed for human use."

Semaglutide: FDA-approved in several products (Drugs@FDA).

  • Ozempic injection (NDA 209637): approved 5 December 2017 for blood-sugar control in adults with type 2 diabetes. A cardiovascular risk-reduction indication for adults with type 2 diabetes and established cardiovascular disease was added on 16 January 2020, and a kidney-outcomes indication for adults with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease on 28 January 2025.
  • Rybelsus tablets (NDA 213051): approved 20 September 2019 for type 2 diabetes. A cardiovascular risk-reduction indication was added on 17 October 2025. On 30 January 2026 the FDA approved renaming one Rybelsus tablet formulation as Ozempic tablets (NDA 213051/S-030).
  • Wegovy injection (NDA 215256): approved 4 June 2021 for chronic weight management in adults. Use in adolescents aged 12 and older followed on 23 December 2022. On 8 March 2024 a cardiovascular risk-reduction indication was added, based on SELECT, and on 15 August 2025 an accelerated approval for noncirrhotic MASH with moderate to advanced fibrosis. On 19 March 2026 the FDA approved a higher weekly maintenance dose for weight reduction.
  • Wegovy tablets (NDA 218316): approved 22 December 2025.
  • In the EU, the European Commission first authorised Ozempic on 8 February 2018, Rybelsus on 3 April 2020 and Wegovy on 6 January 2022 (EMA).

The RUO and compounding context. The FDA states that retatrutide "cannot be used in compounding under federal law" and is not a component of any FDA-approved drug. It also says it has warned companies that sold semaglutide, retatrutide and other GLP-1 drugs "falsely labeled 'for research purposes' or 'not for human consumption'" to consumers. Research-labelled "retatrutide" or "semaglutide" sold online is not the trial material or an approved product. Its identity, purity and contents are not covered by any of the data above. For how approval, compounding and RUO labelling differ, see Are Research Peptides Legal? FDA & RUO Basics.

What the trials don't tell us

  • Company-reported topline only. One head-to-head Phase 3 trial, TRANSCEND-T2D-2 in type 2 diabetes, has company-reported topline results as of 28 Oct 2026 that are not yet peer-reviewed or published. It describes people with type 2 diabetes on metformin, in an open-label design, not people without diabetes.
  • Different durations and eras. The TRIUMPH trials ran 80 weeks and reported in 2026. STEP 1 and STEP 2 ran 68 weeks and reported in 2021.
  • Peer review is partial for retatrutide. TRIUMPH-1 and TRIUMPH-2 have papers. The efficacy rows are reported in those papers and company-reported by Lilly. TRIUMPH-3 figures are company-reported only.
  • Outcomes evidence differs. Semaglutide has a completed cardiovascular outcomes trial in people without diabetes (SELECT) and FDA-approved cardiovascular and kidney risk-reduction indications. Retatrutide's outcomes trial is not expected to complete before 2029.
  • Long-term safety. Semaglutide has been FDA-approved since December 2017. Retatrutide data come only from controlled trials lasting up to about two years.
  • Not about individual response. Trial averages do not predict how one person will respond.

FAQ

Has retatrutide been compared head to head with semaglutide?

Yes, in one trial, but so far only in a company announcement. On 28 Oct 2026, Eli Lilly reported topline results from TRANSCEND-T2D-2, an open-label Phase 3 trial comparing two retatrutide dose arms with once-weekly semaglutide (Ozempic) in adults with type 2 diabetes on metformin [company-reported]. The primary endpoint was noninferiority on A1C change at 80 weeks for the highest retatrutide dose arm versus semaglutide, and Lilly said the trial met it [company-reported]. The results have not been peer-reviewed or fully published, and they apply only to that population. Retatrutide is not approved.

How do retatrutide and semaglutide work differently?

Semaglutide is a modified GLP-1 analogue that activates the GLP-1 receptor only. Retatrutide is a single peptide that activates GIP, GLP-1 and glucagon receptors. Researchers have proposed that the glucagon component may add effects on energy intake or energy expenditure, but this has not been established in humans, and a different mechanism does not by itself make a drug more effective or safer.

Can the TRIUMPH and STEP weight results be compared directly?

No. They are separate placebo-controlled trials that differ in population, duration, era, dose escalation and estimand definitions, and none compared the two drugs with each other. This article reports results within each trial only and does not rank the two drugs.

Why do some retatrutide figures look higher in news coverage?

They usually use a different estimand. In TRIUMPH-1, the efficacy estimand, reported in the paper and company-reported by Lilly, gives a larger mean weight change for the highest dose arm than the treatment-regimen estimand in the NEJM paper. The treatment-regimen estimand counts everyone randomized. The efficacy estimand estimates the effect had everyone stayed on treatment. Both figures, with their sources, are in the TRIUMPH table above.

What side effects were reported in the trials?

For both drugs, gastrointestinal events such as nausea, diarrhoea, vomiting and constipation were the most common. In the TRIUMPH-2 paper, diarrhoea, dysesthesia and hypotension were more frequent in the retatrutide arms than with placebo. In STEP 1, gastrointestinal disorders were more frequent with semaglutide than with placebo. Rates by arm, with their sources, are in the side-effect tables above.

Is retatrutide FDA-approved?

No. As of 19 October 2026, retatrutide is investigational and not approved by the FDA or the EMA. Lilly says it plans to submit it for US approval in the first quarter of 2027. The FDA has determined that retatrutide is a drug rather than a biological product, a classification Lilly is challenging in court.

What is semaglutide approved for?

In the US, Ozempic (injection and tablets) and Rybelsus are approved for type 2 diabetes, with cardiovascular risk-reduction indications and, for Ozempic injection, a kidney-outcomes indication. Wegovy injection is approved for weight management in adults and adolescents aged 12 and older, cardiovascular risk reduction in adults with established cardiovascular disease and obesity or overweight, and MASH with moderate to advanced fibrosis. Wegovy tablets were approved on 22 December 2025.

Is research-labelled retatrutide or semaglutide the same as the trial drugs?

No. Products sold online as research-use-only retatrutide or semaglutide are not the material used in these trials and are not FDA-approved products. The FDA says retatrutide cannot be used in compounding and has warned companies selling GLP-1 drugs falsely labelled for research purposes. This article is educational and is not medical advice.

Eloralintide plus tirzepatide and retatrutide share the same online conversation—multi-pathway obesity research and large percent headlines stacked as if they came from one trial. They did not. This evidence note covers what has been published, which estimand each percent belongs to, and why a combo readout is not a head-to-head with TRIUMPH-1.

What is being compared

Eloralintide is an investigational selective amylin receptor agonist (LY3841136)—an amylin / satiety pathway, not a GLP-1 drug by itself.

Tirzepatide is a dual GIP and GLP-1 receptor agonist. In Lilly’s EloraTZP program, eloralintide and tirzepatide were studied together (separate injections in the disclosed phase 2b design).

Retatrutide is an investigational GIP, GLP-1, and glucagon triple receptor agonist—one molecule, three named pathways.

The online “versus” is amylin agonist + dual incretin versus triple agonist—same neighborhood, different pharmacology and trials.

What is actually published

Eloralintide monotherapy

Phase 2 NCT06230523 (Lancet; Lilly release 6 Nov 2025) enrolled 263 adults with obesity or overweight and at least one weight-related comorbidity, without type 2 diabetes. At 48 weeks, the Lilly release (not the Lancet abstract, which rounds those arms) gives the efficacy estimand mean percent body-weight change as −9.5% (lowest dose arm) to −20.1% (highest dose arm) versus −0.4% placebo. That is monotherapy context for the amylin piece—not the combination.

Eloralintide + tirzepatide (EloraTZP)

The combination package tied to a primary Lilly / EASD release is phase 2b NCT06603571: 367 adults with obesity or overweight and type 2 diabetes, 48 weeks. Lilly’s 30 Sep 2026 release (also via EASD / EurekAlert) reports an efficacy estimand table: highest listed combo arm (eloralintide plus tirzepatide) −23.3%, versus −14.8% for tirzepatide alone and −3.0% placebo. Eloralintide-alone arms in that T2D trial were lower than the top combo. GI events and discontinuations were more frequent in combo arms; Lilly plans phase 3 of a co-formulation with optimized escalation.

Smaller early co-administration cohorts (including NCT06345066 and related phase 1b work) circulate in congress talk and secondary blogs. Those readouts remain preliminary—small arms, shorter follow-up, incomplete evaluable counts in secondary reports. This page does not print an unverified viral percent from that slide-level discussion. Without a checkable Lilly, journal, registry-results, or official congress primary for a specific figure, treat phase 1b combo numbers as exploratory—not a TRIUMPH-1 comparator.

Retatrutide TRIUMPH-1 (no diabetes)

TRIUMPH-1 (NCT05929066; Jastreboff et al., NEJM, DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2604169, PMID 42814954) studied adults with obesity or overweight without type 2 diabetes. At 80 weeks, treatment-regimen estimand mean percent body-weight change in the highest dose arm was −25.0% (lowest dose arm −17.6%, middle dose arm −23.7%, placebo −3.9%). The same trial’s efficacy estimand in the highest dose arm was −28.3% (lowest dose arm −19.0%, middle dose arm −25.9%). These are two estimands of one trial, not two trials. Lead with −25.0% when comparing programs; −28.3% is the efficacy-estimand companion, not a “stale wrong number.”

Retatrutide TRIUMPH-2 (with type 2 diabetes)

TRIUMPH-2 (Bellido et al., Lancet, DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(26)01861-101861-1)) is a different population—adults with type 2 diabetes. At 80 weeks, treatment-regimen estimand in the highest dose arm was −18.8% (placebo −5.1%). Efficacy estimand in the highest dose arm was −20.8% (placebo −4.0% on Lilly Medical). Do not mix TRIUMPH-1 and TRIUMPH-2 toplines as if they were interchangeable.

Why 25.0% and 28.3% can both be true

Obesity trials often pre-specify two estimands:

  • Treatment-regimen (treatment-policy): average effect for randomized participants even if some stop drug or start other weight-loss treatments. TRIUMPH-1’s −25.0% (highest dose arm) sits here.
  • Efficacy estimand: a hypothetical “everyone stayed on assigned intervention without those intercurrent events” contrast. Same TRIUMPH-1 dataset → −28.3% in the highest dose arm.

Both can be true because they answer different questions. Name the estimand every time a percent appears, and prefer the treatment-regimen number when informal ranking is tempting.

Why a small combo readout is not a head-to-head

  1. Population. EloraTZP phase 2b: with type 2 diabetes. TRIUMPH-1: without diabetes. TRIUMPH-2 is the closer population match for the published combo—and still not the same study.
  2. Duration. Combo phase 2b: 48 weeks. TRIUMPH-1 / 2: 80 weeks.
  3. Phase and size. Combination: phase 2b across many arms. TRIUMPH-1: phase 3, thousands randomized. Phase 1b combo cohorts are smaller still.
  4. Intervention. Two injections versus one triple-agonist molecule.
  5. Estimand. Lilly’s EloraTZP table is labeled efficacy estimand. TRIUMPH-1’s −25.0% lead figure is treatment-regimen.

No published head-to-head of the combination versus retatrutide was identified in the primaries checked here. Side-by-side blog tables are editorial layouts, not randomized comparisons.

What is still missing

  • Peer-reviewed full paper for EloraTZP phase 2b beyond company / congress release.
  • Checkable official abstract text for viral phase 1b combo slide figures.
  • Phase 3 co-formulation results (Lilly plans to start late 2026).
  • A true head-to-head versus retatrutide in the same population, duration, and estimand.
  • Treatment-regimen body-weight figures for EloraTZP comparable to TRIUMPH-1’s −25.0% lane.

Until then: retatrutide has large phase 3 packages with labeled estimands; eloralintide has phase 2 monotherapy data; the combo has a phase 2b T2D efficacy-estimand top line of −23.3% at 48 weeks—and early combo work still too thin to stack against TRIUMPH-1.

FAQ

Why can TRIUMPH-1 list both −25.0% and −28.3%?

They are two estimands of one trial in the highest dose arm at 80 weeks in adults without type 2 diabetes. −25.0% is the treatment-regimen estimand. −28.3% is the efficacy estimand. Lead with −25.0% when comparing programs. −28.3% is the efficacy-estimand companion, not a second trial.

What did EloraTZP report for eloralintide plus tirzepatide?

Lilly’s 30 September 2026 release (company-reported, not peer reviewed) reports an efficacy estimand of −23.3% for the highest listed combination of eloralintide plus tirzepatide at 48 weeks, versus −14.8% for tirzepatide alone and −3.0% for placebo, in 367 adults with obesity or overweight and type 2 diabetes.

Is that combination result a head-to-head with TRIUMPH-1?

No. EloraTZP phase 2b included type 2 diabetes, ran 48 weeks, and its table is an efficacy estimand. TRIUMPH-1 excluded diabetes, ran 80 weeks, and its lead figure is a treatment-regimen estimand. No published head-to-head of the combination versus retatrutide was identified.

What did TRIUMPH-2 report?

TRIUMPH-2 enrolled adults with type 2 diabetes, a closer population match for EloraTZP and still a different study. At 80 weeks the highest dose arm treatment-regimen change was −18.8% (placebo −5.1%). The efficacy estimand in the highest dose arm was −20.8% (placebo −4.0% on Lilly Medical).

hhs-503a-peptide-enforcement-discretion-.html:
Peptidemap is a research-use-only (RUO) comparison publisher, not a clinic, pharmacy or supplier. This explainer summarises a regulatory document. It is not medical, legal or purchasing advice.

On 28 Oct 2026, the HHS Office of the Secretary announced a draft "Enforcement Discretion Policy Regarding 503A Compounding Using Certain Peptide Bulk Drug Substances" [1][2] [primary]. The Federal Register notice is FR Doc. 2026-22192 (docket HHS-OASH-2026-0496, RIN 0910-ZD94). It was filed on 28 Oct and published in the Federal Register on 30 Oct 2026 at 91 FR 68526 [2] [primary]. The notice says that, in listed circumstances, "HHS does not intend to take enforcement action against a State-licensed pharmacy, Federal facility, or licensed physician" compounding with the named substances [1] [primary].

The six peptides

Appendix A lists the six peptides. Appendix B limits coverage to specific forms and routes [1] [primary]. The routes below describe the draft's scope only. They are not usage information.

  1. BPC-157: the draft lists the acetate form, for subcutaneous, intramuscular, oral and topical dosage forms.
  2. Epitalon: the draft lists the acetate form, for subcutaneous or intramuscular injectable dosage forms "dispensed in intermittent courses."
  3. KPV: the draft lists the acetate form, for topical and oral dosage forms.
  4. MOTS-c: the draft lists the acetate form, for subcutaneous or intramuscular injectable dosage forms.
  5. Semax: the draft lists the free base, for intranasal use.
  6. TB-500: the draft lists the acetate form, for subcutaneous or intramuscular injectable dosage forms only.

Other conditions also apply [1] [primary]:

  • The product must contain a single listed active ingredient, so blends are outside the draft.
  • The drug must be compounded under a valid patient-specific prescription.
  • The ingredient must come from a 510-registered, CGMP-compliant original manufacturer and carry a COA that meets FDA-referenced testing criteria.
  • Serious adverse events and product-quality issues must be reported to FDA's MedWatch and to the relevant States.
  • The label must read "This is a compounded drug product. Not for resale."

For the full conditions, and for how this differs from RUO-labelled products, see our guide Compounded vs RUO Peptides. For background, see Are Research Peptides Legal? FDA & RUO Basics.

Timeline

  • 22 Apr 2026. Appendix B says each of the six left FDA's interim Category 2 on this date. None is in Category 1 [1] [primary].
  • 23–24 Jul 2026. FDA's Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee met [4] [primary]. Appendix B records that "CDER recommended against listing" each peptide and that the PCAC voted in favour [1] [primary]. NPR reported that FDA's own scientists recommended against unwinding the restrictions [5] [press].
  • 14 Oct 2026. OIRA received the item for review under RIN 0910-ZD94, titled "Interim Access Policy for Compounding Using Certain Peptides" [3] [primary].
  • 27 Oct 2026. OIRA concluded its review "Consistent with Change" [3] [primary].
  • 28 Oct 2026. HHS announced the policy, and the Federal Register notice was filed [2] [primary].
  • 30 Oct 2026. Federal Register publication at 91 FR 68526–68527. Comments are open "until 2 weeks after date of publication" [2] [primary]. Regulations.gov lists the comment period as closing on 13 Nov 2026 at 11:59 pm Eastern Time [7] [primary].

What it is, and what is still pending

The notice calls the policy a "draft" and says it "does not establish any rights for any person and is not binding on HHS or the public" [2] [primary]. It is not approval: "Compounded drugs are not FDA-approved" [1][2] [primary]. None of the six is on the 503A Bulks List [1] [primary]. The draft has no end date. It applies "until a peptide bulk drug substance is addressed in a final rule," and HHS "may revisit" it if "a safety signal or product quality issue arises" [1] [primary].

Several things are still pending:

  • The comment period, which Regulations.gov lists as closing on 13 Nov 2026 [7] [primary], and any revision to the draft [2] [primary].
  • Rulemaking. "FDA's future rulemakings may propose adding some or all of these peptides to the 503A bulks list" [2] [primary]. NCPA reports that pharmacies "are still awaiting final rulemaking" [6] [press].
  • Supply. NPR quotes a compounder who said "We won't be able to meet demand" [5] [press].

HHS presents the draft as a way to "discourage the continued, widespread use of certain research-use-only peptides supplied by foreign manufacturers that pose a safety risk to US patients" [1] [primary]. That is HHS's framing. The documents make no safety or efficacy finding for any of the six.

FAQ

Is this an FDA approval?

No. The issuer is the HHS Office of the Secretary, and the notice says compounded drugs are not FDA-approved [2] [primary].

Is it final?

No. It is a draft, interim, non-binding policy with a two-week comment window [2] [primary].

Are blends covered?

No. The draft requires a single listed active ingredient [1] [primary].

Does it cover RUO-labelled products?

No. Its terms require 503A compounding, a patient-specific prescription and registered CGMP sourcing [1] [primary].

bpc-157-vs-ghk-cu.html:
BPC-157 and GHK-Cu often sit side by side in "skin and recovery" catalog sections, and some blend vials contain both. They are unrelated molecules. BPC-157 is a synthetic 15-amino-acid peptide studied mostly in rodents. GHK-Cu is a copper complex of a naturally occurring tripeptide, and most of its human data are topical and cosmetic.

Peptidemap is an RUO / grey-area peptide comparison publisher, not a clinic, pharmacy, or supplier. This article is educational. It is not medical advice, does not cover dosing, protocols, or reconstitution, and does not rank the two.

What each is

FDA's July 2026 briefing lists BPC-157 free base as CAS 137525-51-0 with the same formula and weight, and calls it "not well-characterized" physically and chemically. Salt forms such as acetate change the formula and mass, so a label should say which form it means. GHK-Cu has a similar problem: copper-free "GHK" is sold separately, and a 2026 review in Pharmaceutics (Mateescu et al.) notes the literature "frequently treats GHK-Cu as a single active ingredient" even though copper binding and free copper vary by formulation.

Peptidemap's compound hubs are BPC-157 and GHK-Cu.

Proposed mechanisms (research hypotheses)

Everything below comes from cell and animal research. A proposed pathway is not proof of effect in people.

BPC-157. FDA's 2026 briefing summarizes the hypotheses: researchers have proposed that BPC-157 may "up-regulate the expression of growth factors and their receptors, suppress release and/or expression of inflammatory factors, induce angiogenesis, and stimulate nitric oxide synthesis." It adds that "the molecular targets for BPC-157-related substances have not been identified."

GHK-Cu. The two Pickart reviews cited here list Skin Biology, a copper-peptide skincare company founded by Loren Pickart, as the authors' affiliation; Pickart (1938–2023) first isolated GHK in 1973. Those reviews propose that the complex supports collagen and glycosaminoglycan synthesis, modulates matrix-degrading enzymes and their inhibitors, and shifts expression of large gene sets. The independent 2026 Mateescu review says preclinical data "consistently support" effects on matrix remodeling, epithelial repair, inflammatory and redox signaling, and angiogenesis, but "the clinical evidence remains sparse."

Evidence base side by side

Evidence layerBPC-157GHK-Cu
Cell and animalLarge rodent literature (GI, tendon, ligament, muscle)Fibroblast, wound, and gene-expression work; animal wound models
Human, topicalNot the main research lineSmall cosmetic and dermatology studies with mixed results
Human, injected or systemicA few small uncontrolled pilot reportsNo published controlled trial identified
Systematic review signal2025 review: 36 studies, 35 preclinical and 1 clinical2026 review: clinical evidence "sparse"

BPC-157 human data. A 2025 systematic review in HSS Journal (Vasireddi et al.) included 36 studies (35 preclinical, 1 clinical) and found no clinical safety data. A 2025 narrative review (McGuire et al.) called human data "extremely limited," citing three pilot studies. Examples are an uncontrolled 12-patient interstitial cystitis series and a 2-person intravenous safety pilot. FDA's 2026 briefing found "insufficient clinical safety information to characterize the safety profile" of BPC-157.

GHK-Cu human data. These are mostly topical, with mixed results.

  • In a 13-patient randomized study after CO2 laser resurfacing (Miller et al., 2006), GHK-Cu products showed no objective difference versus the regimen without GHK-Cu in redness, wrinkles, or skin quality, though patient satisfaction was higher.
  • In an 86-patient randomized trial in venous leg ulcers (Bishop et al., 1992), a "tripeptide copper complex" cream did no better than placebo. The abstract does not name the tripeptide.
  • The Mateescu review cites a 2026 split-face eyebrow study in 18 participants that reported positive cosmetic hair results without defining GHK-Cu speciation.
  • A placebo-controlled phase 2 trial of a topical GHK-Cu gel for acute skin wounds (NCT07437586) is recruiting and has no results yet.

Topical vs injectable: keep them separate

Cosmetic studies measure appearance outcomes for a specific cream or serum on skin. They do not establish what happens when GHK-Cu is injected, where exposure, copper release, and immunogenicity are different questions. FDA lists GHK-Cu "for injectable routes of administration" with the note that injectable products "may pose risk for immunogenicity due to the potential for aggregation and peptide-related impurities" and that "there are limited data in humans."

Hair claims need care too: a frequently cited follicle paper (Pyo et al., 2007) tested AHK-Cu, a different copper tripeptide, in cultured follicles, not GHK-Cu in people. BPC-157 has no comparable topical evidence line.

Regulatory and legal status (checked October 2026)

FDA approval. Neither compound is an FDA-approved drug. For how approval, 503A compounding, and RUO labels differ, see Are research peptides legal? FDA, RUO & compounding explained and FDA peptide reclassification 2026.

Compounding (BPC-157). FDA's page on bulk substances that may present significant safety risks (content current as of 22 April 2026) lists BPC-157 in the table of substances "previously in category 2" whose nominations "were withdrawn by the nominators." FDA kept its concerns (immunogenicity, impurities, and "no, or only limited, safety-related information"). Off Category 2 is not permission to compound. FDA's 503A categories list (updated 14 May 2026) places BPC-157 in neither Category 1 nor Category 2. For the July 23–24, 2026 Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (PCAC) meeting, FDA staff reviewed BPC-157 for ulcerative colitis and proposed not adding it to the 503A Bulks List. The committee voted to recommend inclusion anyway (BMJ reporting); FDA calls such recommendations non-binding. In a 1 October 2026 Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health Q&A, Professor S. Bryn Austin said FDA "has not yet announced if it will accept or reject the committee's recommendation." On 7 October 2026 the Washington Post reported, citing unnamed sources, that the administration was crafting plans to allow the temporary sale of certain previously restricted peptides through compounding pharmacies. The plan had not been announced. As of 11 October 2026, no FDA or HHS announcement of such a plan, no proposed rule, and no final 503A listing for BPC-157 was identified.

Compounding (GHK-Cu). The same FDA page lists GHK-Cu (for injectable routes of administration) in that withdrawn-nomination table, with its safety concerns kept. Non-injectable GHK-Cu is handled separately: FDA's 503A categories list (updated 14 May 2026) puts "GHK-Cu (except for injectable routes of administration)" back in Category 1, "under evaluation," after one nominator said it meant to withdraw only the injectable route. Category 1 is an interim review status, not a 503A Bulks List listing and not FDA approval. FDA's PCAC page lists GHK-Cu for discussion at a meeting to be held "before the end of February 2027." A scheduled discussion is not a listing.

Cosmetic status (GHK-Cu). FDA says cosmetic ingredients other than color additives need no premarket approval, and intended use decides whether a product is a cosmetic or a drug. Copper tripeptide-1 in a serum does not make an injectable vial a cosmetic or an approved drug.

RUO labels. In an August 2026 warning letter to Peptide Partners LLC, FDA found products were intended as drugs for human use despite "for research use only" labeling.

WADA (2026 and 2027 lists). BPC-157 is named under S0 Non-approved substances, prohibited at all times. GHK-Cu is not named. S0 is a catch-all for substances without human therapeutic approval, so athletes should ask their anti-doping organization. The 2027 List (effective 1 January 2027) adds "peptides" to S0's examples of non-approved substances; BPC-157 remains named and GHK-Cu still is not.

What a CoA can and can't tell you

A certificate of analysis can show whether the submitted sample's mass matches the label (average molecular weight about 1419.5 g/mol for BPC-157 free base) and what HPLC purity it had under that lab's method. For GHK-Cu, a useful CoA would also report copper content. The Mateescu review notes that copper occupancy and free copper are usually not resolved in delivery studies.

It cannot show that other lots match, that a vial is sterile or endotoxin-free unless tested, or that the compound is safe, effective, or legal for any use. See How to verify a peptide vendor Certificate of Analysis and our testing labs directory. Vendor and price listings are on the BPC-157 vs GHK-Cu compare page. See also BPC-157 vs TB-500: what the evidence shows.

FAQ

Are BPC-157 and GHK-Cu related?

No. BPC-157 is a synthetic 15-amino-acid peptide. GHK-Cu is the copper complex of the naturally occurring tripeptide Gly-His-Lys. They have different sequences, sizes, and research histories.

How does the human evidence differ?

They have different kinds of human evidence. GHK-Cu has small topical cosmetic studies with mixed results. BPC-157 has a few small uncontrolled pilot reports. Neither has controlled trials establishing efficacy for injected use.

Do GHK-Cu skin cream studies apply to injected GHK-Cu?

No. Topical studies test a specific formulation on skin. They do not establish safety or effects for injection, and FDA notes limited human data for injectable GHK-Cu.

Is BPC-157 still on FDA's Category 2 list?

FDA's page now lists BPC-157 among nominations withdrawn from Category 2, with its safety concerns kept. A July 2026 advisory committee recommended it for the 503A Bulks List, but as of October 2026 no final FDA listing was identified.

Is GHK-Cu legal because it is in cosmetics?

Cosmetic ingredients do not need FDA premarket approval, but intended use decides whether a product is a cosmetic or a drug. A cosmetic serum's status does not make an injectable vial an approved drug.

Are they banned in sport?

BPC-157 is named under S0 on the WADA 2026 Prohibited List and remains named on the 2027 List. GHK-Cu is not named on either, but S0 covers unapproved substances generally, and the 2027 List adds peptides to its examples, so athletes should check with their anti-doping organization.
